messages.content: You are a clinical documentation assistant that runs entirely on local hardware. You help clinicians summarize encounter notes, write structured SOAP notes, and extract medical entities. Use only information stated in the provided note. Never invent findings, diagnoses, medications, doses, or plans, and preserve negations exactly (for example, a symptom the patient denies must not be reported as present).

Summarize the following clinical encounter note for a busy clinician.
Requirements:
- Write 3 to 6 sentences of plain prose (maximum 120 words), in the third person.
- Cover the patient's age/sex and reason for the visit, the key history and findings, the assessment, and the plan.
- Use only information stated in the note. Do not use headings or bullet points.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: so [NAME] is a 45 -year-old male who came in today with an ankle injury [NAME] what happened
Patient: hey doctor [NAME] yeah so my son [NAME] i think you met in the past he he started playing basketball and there we do multiple seasons and so we're kinda getting ready for the next season that starts in in april and we were at the courts plan and i went up for a shot and he's far more aggressive than with me than he is with you know his peers i guess he could say and so he he found me while i was going for a lap and then when i came down i kind of landed awkwardly and i kind of like rolled and twisted my my ankle so now it's it's hurting a bit like kind of on the outside you can you can even see it's it's bruised up and a bit swollen
Doctor: yeah
Patient: and yeah i've been having trouble walking and it just does n't feel solid really stable which is a problem i i recently got back into working out and i had been in a really good rhythm going to the gym
Doctor: okay
Patient: and i do n't want to disrupt that moments on because it took a lot for me to get back to a good place so
Doctor: absolutely okay totally understand that glad to hear that you're back out on the court playing with your son how is he doing by the way
Patient: he is doing great he is doing great i mean you know he is a big step kurry fan so he likes to keep up shots from from way out past the three point line and he is only ten and tiny so it's it's not a good idea for him to do that but he is doing really well and i'm just happy he's tried every sport and basketball's really what took so i'm just really happy that he has a sport and loves and couple of his buddies playing to lead with him so it's just makes me happy that he's found something he really enjoys
Doctor: good good to hear alright well let's take a look at that ankle it looks like it's pretty swollen so let me just do a quick exam on that right now alright so looks like the outside of your ankle if i push on that does that hurt pretty bad
Patient: yeah yes
Doctor: okay so exquisite tenderness tenderness laterally and then if i push here does that hurt too
Patient: yeah a little bit
Doctor: okay so some tenderness over the medial deltoid region so swelling on the lateral side of the ankle no epidermolysis skin is intact looks like you have brisk capillary refill no horrible malalignment so alright can you can you stand on it did you say that you're having trouble walking at all
Patient: yeah i mean i can stand on it and i ca n't walk on it it just it hurts and it feels like i'm going to possibly injure it more just because it does n't feel particularly solid
Doctor: sure so it does n't quite feel stable
Patient: yeah
Doctor: okay okay i gotcha so i know you had an x-ray as you came in today and so i'm just looking at this x-ray here i'll show you on the screen right here i can turn my monitor towards you this is an ap lateral oblique and this is your right ankle so what we're looking at is a displaced lateral malleolus at the weber c level there's no evidence of medial or posterior malleolar fractures but this is a fracture on the lateral side of your ankle now based on the position it's a bit unstable that's why you're feeling some of that that instability when you're walking so for your diagnosis what i'm gon na put down is a lateral malleolar fracture and what i would recommend for that since it is in the location that it is is you're probably unfortunately gon na need surgery we're gon na wan na get that healed what that includes is putting some plate and some screws in and you're gon na be out for a little bit so i know you've been trying to work out and and you wan na get back on the court but but you may have to have to sit out for a little bit we'll get you some crutches
Patient: how long it's a little bit because i'm also i i forgot to say i'm also i did volunteer to coach
Doctor: great
Patient: starting in april so
Doctor: alright well
Patient: how long
Doctor: yeah you you're probably gon na be out for about three months but continue the coaching go ahead and and let's get you back out there we'll get you some crutches and and hopefully you can kinda you know get back on the court start coaching and then within that three months we'll we'll get you back out doing some exercise again
Patient: okay
Doctor: alright in the meantime i'm gon na prescribe some medication for now let's try meloxicam and try to get some of the swelling down i want you to ice it and also keep that that ankle elevated do you have a job where you can elevate your ankle regularly
Patient: yeah i i work from home so that that should n't be a problem it's just everything else i do n't know who is gon na walk my dogs and and do all this stuff that's rest of my family refuses to walk my dog so we'll figure it out
Doctor: yeah i i'm a dog walker as well so alright sorry for the bad news but let's get you healed up so that we can get you back out doing everything you need to do
Patient: alright thank you doctor
Doctor: alright thanks
"""

reference:
SUBJECTIVE:
The patient presents with a chief complaint of acid reflux. She reports a long-standing history of symptoms since age 12, with worsening in recent years. She describes a burning sensation in her chest and throat. She denies dysphagia, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movements, constipation, diarrhea, or rectal bleeding. She has unintentionally had a poor appetite for the past 2 months due to work-related stress. She identifies trigger foods including spicy foods, soda, citrus, and tomato-based products, though she admits to still consuming them occasionally. She has been taking omeprazole 40 mg twice daily for approximately 1 year, which provides partial relief. She previously took ranitidine in combination with omeprazole, which she felt helped. She denies an upper endoscopy in the last 10 years. Past medical history includes anxiety and seasonal allergies. Surgical history includes infant surgery for twisted intestines. She works as a paralegal. Family history includes maternal grandmother with esophageal cancer.

OBJECTIVE:
Physical examination reveals a well-healed abdominal surgical scar. No other pertinent findings.

ASSESSMENT:
The patient has a several-year history of GERD, primarily manifesting as heartburn, which is poorly controlled with omeprazole 40 mg twice daily. She has identified multiple triggers for her symptoms. There is no evidence of unintentional weight loss or dysphagia. GERD with suspected underlying functional etiology is suspected.

PLAN:
1. Recommend dietary and lifestyle modifications, including avoidance of trigger foods and stress reduction.
2. Prescribe Nexium 40 mg twice daily to replace current omeprazole 40 mg twice daily.
3. Recommend an upper endoscopy (EGD) to evaluate for potential causes of GERD.
4. If EGD is normal and symptoms persist despite Nexium, consider a trial of Protonix and obtain a pH impedance study to differentiate between functional etiology and hypersensitivity.
5. Counsel the patient to contact the office if symptoms change or worsen prior to EGD or follow-up.
6. Schedule a follow-up visit after the EGD to discuss results and assess response to treatment.

Patient: you as well .
Doctor: how can i help you today ?
Patient: well , my primary doctor , dr. [NAME] , he referred me here .
Doctor: okay .
Patient: i've just got really bad acid reflux .
Doctor: okay . can you tell me more about it ?
Patient: yeah . though i mean i ... right now , i take 40 milligrams of omeprazole twice a day . some days , it is fine , but others are just really bad .

Patient: it feels like burning .

Patient: yes , in my chest and also in my throat .
Doctor: in your throat and chest . all right . any difficulty with swallowing ? feels like food or liquids kinda get stuck ?
Patient: no .

Patient: no , not really .
Doctor: nausea or vomiting , changes in bowel movements ?
Patient: no .
Doctor: constipation , diarrhea , rectal bleeding ?
Patient: nope .
Doctor: okay . very good . and how long have you had this problem ?
Patient: i've had acid reflux since i was around 12 , but it has gotten worse over the past few years .
Doctor: okay . and how long have you been on the omeprazole ?
Patient: on the way , it is now i think about a year .
Doctor: okay . do you find that it's done anything for you in the past ?
Patient: i mean , i can tell it's helped because some days , i'll be fine , and then some days , i eat something and it feels terrible .

Doctor: okay . what things bother you ?
Patient: spicy foods , um , so i try not to eat them too often , but sometimes even drinking a soda can cause it .
Doctor: we do know that caffeine and caffeinated beverages will do that , even sodas . um , even just the carbonation can cause that . how about tomato-based products or citrus products ?
Patient: yeah , sometimes , but i still eat them .
Doctor: okay . it's reassuring that you are n't having any difficulty swallowing , though . how's your weight been ? pretty stable ?
Patient: i'd say pretty stable , although i have n't had much of an appetite for the past two months . i have been under a lot of work stress .
Doctor: what do you do for work ?
Patient: i'm a paralegal .
Doctor: okay . and any family history of gi issues ?
Patient: um , my grandmother had esophageal cancer .
Doctor: on your mom or dad's side ?

Doctor: okay . have you ever had an upper endoscopy ?

Patient: okay .

Patient: yes .
Doctor: and you've identified trigger foods like spicy foods , carbonated bev- beverages , citrus , and tomato-based foods , but you have n't cut these foods out of your diet completely yet . so the first thing i'd try is changing your diet because these foods can exacerbate your gerd , even though you're taking the ppi .
Patient: okay , yeah , i could definitely do a better job of avoiding those foods .
Doctor: great . so stress is another trigger that we need to address . high stress can cause worsening of your symptoms .
Patient: yeah , stress and anxiety are definitely big problems for me .
Doctor: so working on that may help with your gerd . additionally , we can consider trying a different ppi since the only one you've tried up to this point is omeprazole . if you're okay with this , we can switch your omeprazole to nexium .
Patient: that's fine with me . i'm definitely open to trying whatever .

Patient: okay . can i schedule that today ?
Doctor: yeah . you can get scheduled at checkout desk . i'll have you follow up with me in the office for the egd so we can discuss the results and talk about how you're doing with the dietary , stress , and medication changes . how does all of that sound ?
Patient: that sounds good .
Doctor: perfect . i will walk you to the checkout desk . be sure to call my office and let me know if anything changes or if you have problems before your egd and follow-up appointment .
Doctor: please insert the procedure paragraph in the plan . i suspect that she likely has gerd with underlying functional etiology as well . reassuringly , she has no unintentional weight loss and denies any dysphagia . if her egd is normal and her symptoms pers- persist despite a trial of nexium , we can consider a trial of protonix and obtain a ph-impedance study . this will allow us to rule out abnormal acid reflux exposure and to decipher between a functional etiology and hypersensitivity .
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: So, you are here to review your sleep study results, right?
Patient: That's right.
Doctor: First let's go back to your medical history a little bit and then we will continue with the result. Patient: Sure.
Doctor: So, you first came to our Pulmonary Clinic, and you were suffering with dyspnea even on minimal exertion. At that time, we evaluated you and we realized that there was some evidence of irregular sleep and daytime fatigue. At that time you also complained of nighttime choking episodes which got less intense over the past many months.
Patient: That's right. I was then scheduled for the overnight sleep study to be evaluated for interruptions in my sleep and here we are today to discuss results.
Doctor: Sure. But first tell me, how is your sleeping routine like?
Patient: It is consistent. I go to bed anytime between nine to ten at night and wake up in the morning around five to six.
Doctor: Are you able to sleep as soon as you go to bed?
Patient: No, it's hard for me to start that sleeping process and then I'm awake in like every one or two hours throughout the night. I keep on tossing and turning throughout the night. I always find my sheets out of order when I wake up.
Doctor: How would you compare your sleep here in the lab and at your home?
Patient: I would say I slept better in the laboratory than I do at home.
Doctor: How do you feel when you wake up in the morning?
Patient: Honestly, I feel tired. Sometimes I also have this dull headache.
Doctor: Do you snore?
Patient: I don't know for myself, but yeah, my daughter was teasing me another day that I was snoring and was talking in my sleep.
Doctor: Did you ever feel that you have difficulty breathing while you are asleep?
Patient: No. But I used to cough a lot in the middle of the night.
Doctor: You said you used to, so it is not anymore?
Patient: Yeah, I haven't been coughing for the last few weeks.
Doctor: How's your daily routine? Do you nap in the daytime?
Patient: I spent a lot of time reading and watching T V. Sometimes I doze off while doing that. Not regular, but I do take nap sometimes in between two to three in afternoon and also in the evening hours.
Doctor: Do you smoke?
Patient: Oh yes, I take around one to two packs of cigarettes each day mainly after dinner.
Doctor: Have you noticed any change in your weight?
Patient: My weight always keeps fluctuating. I remember I was at my maximum weight of two hundred and sixty pounds around one year ago.
Doctor: If that was your maximum how is your weight now?
Patient: Now it is down by approximately thirty pounds.
Doctor: So, for your health care, you are coming here in the outpatient psychiatry and also going to your maintenance clinic, right?
Patient: Yes, that's right.
Doctor: Your current medications include Methadone, Trazodone, and Seroquel.
Patient: That sounds right.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: How are you feeling today, sir?
Patient: I feel pretty weak right now, but I am doing okay at the moment.
Doctor: I reviewed the chart notes that was sent to me by the nursing home. They also sent me your medical history. You have been going through a lot recently.
Patient: Yes, I have. They moved me into the nursing home after I was released from the hospital. I hope that it is just temporary.
Doctor: I understand that you had a seizer and that is why you were taken to the hospital.
Patient: I had multiple seizures. After I was stabilized from the last seizure this side of my body in not working right.
Doctor: Okay so you are having some partial weakness on this side?
Patient: Yes. That is why they moved me to the nursing home. I can't stand up. I am too weak. I can't take care of myself. The nurses have to help me do everything.
Doctor: I am going to try to help you get back to doing things on your own.
Patient: After being in the hospital I got an infection in my intestines. They put me on some antibiotic that I have never heard of and a probiotic.
Doctor: Okay. I see here in the chart that you had two surgeries on July sixth.
Patient: Yes, and then I had a radiation treatment too.
Doctor: Oh yes. On August seventh.
Patient: That sounds right.
Doctor: Your surgeries may have been the reason for the C diff.
Patient: What is C diff?
Doctor: It is an infection in the large intestine. It is often caused by overuse of antibiotics, and you have been on them for a while due to the surgeries that you have had. Or it could be from the surgery itself.
Patient: That make since.
"""

He also experienced a C diff infection after surgeries and radiation treatment. The doctor discusses possible causes of the C diff and plans to help the patient regain independence.

Family medicine inpatient progress note, hospital day 2. The patient is a 41-year-old female with type 2 diabetes who was admitted with acute bacterial sinusitis after failing outpatient oral antibiotic treatment. Her sister, who lives with her and acts as her caregiver, was present at the bedside and provided part of the history because the patient is exhausted and has a hoarse voice.

Her sister reports 12 days of facial pain and thick green nasal drainage that seemed to improve after about five days and then worsened, with fevers up to 102 F at home over the past two days and poor oral intake. The patient adds that she has pressure over the left cheek, a frontal headache, nasal congestion, and a cough that is worse at night. She denies vision changes, double vision, eye swelling, neck stiffness, and confusion. She completed five days of amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily as an outpatient without improvement. She has no known drug allergies.

Since admission she was started on ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every six hours. She is also using fluticasone nasal spray, 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, saline nasal irrigation, and acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed. Her home metformin 1000 mg twice daily was held, and she is covered with sliding-scale insulin while she is eating poorly. Overnight her maximum temperature was 100.8 F.

Vital signs this morning: temperature 99.1 F, blood pressure 118/72, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On exam she has tenderness over the left maxillary and frontal sinuses, purulent drainage from the left middle meatus, and erythematous nasal mucosa. There is no periorbital edema, extraocular movements are intact, the neck is supple, and the lungs are clear. WBC is 14.2 and fingerstick glucose is 168 mg/dL. CT of the sinuses shows an air-fluid level in the left maxillary sinus and mucosal thickening of the left ethmoid sinuses without orbital or intracranial extension.

My impression is acute bacterial sinusitis that failed outpatient amoxicillin, without orbital or intracranial complication, in a patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus. We will continue ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every six hours today. If she is afebrile and eating tomorrow, we will switch to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg/125 mg twice daily to complete ten days of therapy. Continue fluticasone, saline irrigation, and acetaminophen. Metformin will stay on hold until she is eating normally, with glucose checks before meals. Her sister was updated and understands the plan. Encourage fluids and rest.

Clinical note:
"""
Family medicine inpatient progress note, hospital day 2. The patient is a 41-year-old female with type 2 diabetes who was admitted with acute bacterial sinusitis after failing outpatient oral antibiotic treatment. Her sister, who lives with her and acts as her caregiver, was present at the bedside and provided part of the history because the patient is exhausted and has a hoarse voice.

Her sister reports 12 days of facial pain and thick green nasal drainage that seemed to improve after about five days and then worsened, with fevers up to 102 F at home over the past two days and poor oral intake. The patient adds that she has pressure over the left cheek, a frontal headache, nasal congestion, and a cough that is worse at night. She denies vision changes, double vision, eye swelling, neck stiffness, and confusion. She completed five days of amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily as an outpatient without improvement. She has no known drug allergies.

Since admission she was started on ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every six hours. She is also using fluticasone nasal spray, 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, saline nasal irrigation, and acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed. Her home metformin 1000 mg twice daily was held, and she is covered with sliding-scale insulin while she is eating poorly. Overnight her maximum temperature was 100.8 F.

Vital signs this morning: temperature 99.1 F, blood pressure 118/72, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On exam she has tenderness over the left maxillary and frontal sinuses, purulent drainage from the left middle meatus, and erythematous nasal mucosa. There is no periorbital edema, extraocular movements are intact, the neck is supple, and the lungs are clear. WBC is 14.2 and fingerstick glucose is 168 mg/dL. CT of the sinuses shows an air-fluid level in the left maxillary sinus and mucosal thickening of the left ethmoid sinuses without orbital or intracranial extension.

My impression is acute bacterial sinusitis that failed outpatient amoxicillin, without orbital or intracranial complication, in a patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus. We will continue ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every six hours today. If she is afebrile and eating tomorrow, we will switch to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg/125 mg twice daily to complete ten days of therapy. Continue fluticasone, saline irrigation, and acetaminophen. Metformin will stay on hold until she is eating normally, with glucose checks before meals. Her sister was updated and understands the plan. Encourage fluids and rest.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Visit type: Video visit (live audio and video) for follow-up of alcohol use disorder in a 73-year-old female. She is at home alone, her identity was verified, and she consented to the telehealth visit.

History (patient-reported): She has been in treatment for alcohol use disorder for four months. She reports that her drinking has fallen from about three glasses of wine every night to one or two glasses on about three nights a week, and her last drink was three days ago. Cravings are less intense. She continues naltrexone 50 mg daily without nausea or headache. She reports low mood and poor sleep since her husband died last year, sleeping about four to five hours a night. She takes zolpidem 5 mg at bedtime most nights and admits she sometimes takes it after drinking wine. She is also taking sertraline 50 mg daily and lisinopril 10 mg daily for a history of hypertension. She denies tremor, sweats, seizures, blackouts, and falls. She denies suicidal thoughts. A PHQ-9 completed on the patient portal before the visit scored 9.

Home measurements: BP 128/76 and pulse 72 on her home cuff this morning. She reports her weight is stable.

Visual exam by video: Alert and well groomed. Speech is normal in rate with no slurring. No visible tremor in the hands. She describes her mood as low but better, her affect is congruent and mildly constricted, and her thought process is linear. No psychomotor agitation and no signs of intoxication.

Data: Liver tests drawn last week showed AST 34, ALT 29, and GGT 48.

Impression: Alcohol use disorder, improving on naltrexone with reduced consumption. Mild depressive symptoms and insomnia. Combining zolpidem with alcohol is risky at her age.

Next steps: Continue naltrexone 50 mg daily. Increase sertraline from 50 mg to 75 mg daily for the depressive symptoms. Stop zolpidem and use sleep hygiene measures, with a referral for cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia. Refer her to the outpatient addiction program for weekly counseling and encourage a mutual-help group. Repeat liver tests in four weeks. Follow up by video visit in four weeks. She was given the crisis line number and told to go to the emergency department for suicidal thoughts, seizures, or severe shaking if she stops drinking suddenly.
"""

Video exam showed no tremor or intoxication, her PHQ-9 was 9, and liver tests were normal. The impression is improving alcohol use disorder with mild depressive symptoms and insomnia. The plan is to continue naltrexone, increase sertraline to 75 mg, stop zolpidem, refer to counseling, and follow up in four weeks.

Clinical note:
"""
Hospitalist progress note dictation, hospital day 3, correction, hospital day 2. This is a 49-year-old female admitted with acute kidney injury from dehydration after three days of vomiting and watery diarrhea, presumed viral gastroenteritis. Her only chronic condition is hypertension. No acute events overnight. She says the vomiting has stopped and she had one loose stool yesterday, and she is tolerating a regular diet. She denies abdominal pain, fever, blood in the stool, and flank pain. She is very anxious this morning and asked many questions about whether her kidneys are permanently damaged, whether she will need dialysis, and when she can go home. I spent extra time answering each one and reassured her that this kind of injury usually recovers with fluids.

Current medications are normal saline at 125 mL per hour, and her home lisinopril 20 mg daily remains on hold since admission.

Vitals this morning, temperature 98.1, heart rate 82, down from 108 on admission, blood pressure 124/74, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Urine output was 1.4 liters over the last 24 hours. On exam her mucous membranes are moist, lungs are clear, abdomen is soft and nontender, and there is no edema.

Labs this morning, creatinine 1.2, down from 2.1 on admission, with a baseline of 0.8. BUN 24, potassium 3.9, bicarbonate 22. Admission urinalysis showed concentrated urine without blood or protein.

My impression is prerenal acute kidney injury from dehydration, improving, and hypertension. Going forward, continue normal saline until this evening, then stop and encourage oral fluids. Continue holding lisinopril until the creatinine returns to baseline. Repeat basic metabolic panel in the morning, avoid NSAIDs, and if the creatinine keeps improving she can go home tomorrow with repeat labs in one week.
"""

The vomiting has stopped, she denies abdominal pain, fever, blood in the stool, and flank pain, and she was very anxious and asked many questions, which were answered. Creatinine improved to 1.2 from 2.1 on admission, with a baseline of 0.8, and heart rate fell from 108 to 82. The assessment was improving prerenal acute kidney injury from dehydration. Normal saline continues until this evening, lisinopril stays on hold, a basic metabolic panel will be repeated in the morning, and discharge is possible tomorrow.

Clinical note:
"""
Dermatology clinic follow-up for a 48-year-old female with moderate plaque psoriasis treated with adalimumab, seen for a flare. She was diagnosed about 5 years ago and has had a good response to adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks for the past 18 months, with clear skin until about 2 months ago. Over the past 6 weeks the plaques have returned on her elbows, knees, lower back, and scalp with itching, and her fingernails have started to pit again. She traveled in Southeast Asia for 3 weeks and returned 10 days ago. When I asked about her last injection she first said it was 2 weeks ago, but after checking her pharmacy app she corrected herself: her last adalimumab dose was 5 weeks ago, because she left her pens behind during the trip and missed two doses. The last dose was therefore 5 weeks ago, not 2.

She reports mild traveler's diarrhea early in the trip that resolved on its own without antibiotics. She denies fever, cough, night sweats, weight loss, joint pain, joint swelling, and any new rash outside her psoriasis, and no one at home is sick. She received no vaccines before the trip.

Her other conditions are hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia. Her medicines are lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily, triamcinolone 0.1% cream twice daily to the plaques, which has not helped, and calcipotriene-betamethasone foam, which she has been using only twice a week on her scalp. Current medications are hydroxychloroquine 200 mg once daily, which she has taken for years, amlodipine 5 mg daily for hypertension, and pantoprazole 40 mg daily started on admission for stomach protection while on high-dose steroids. Methylprednisolone 40 mg IV daily was given for the first three days. Mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily was started yesterday.

Vitals today: Temp 36.9 C, BP 138/76, HR 76, RR 16, SpO2 96% on room air. She is comfortable. There is a faint malar erythema that is fading. No oral ulcers. There is mild synovitis with swelling and tenderness in the MCP joints of both hands and the left wrist, involving fewer joints than on admission. Lungs are clear, the heart is regular with no rub, and there is no edema.

My assessment is a systemic lupus erythematosus flare with polyarthritis and mucocutaneous involvement, improving on steroids, plus new proteinuria that is concerning for lupus nephritis. Her creatinine is near baseline.

For management, I am changing methylprednisolone to prednisone 40 mg by mouth daily today, with a planned taper of 5 mg per week once her symptoms and labs allow. Continue hydroxychloroquine 200 mg once daily, which is appropriate for her weight and kidney function, and she should have an annual retinal exam. Continue mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily and monitor her blood counts. Continue pantoprazole 40 mg daily while on steroids and continue amlodipine 5 mg daily. Nephrology consult to consider a renal biopsy. Repeat creatinine and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio in two days. Physical therapy for hand and wrist range of motion. Anticipate discharge in two to three days with rheumatology clinic follow-up in one week.
"""

Underuse of apixaban because of cost raises his stroke risk with atrial fibrillation. Hypertension and diabetes appear controlled.

Plan is to stop oxybutynin and diphenhydramine, and to use timed voiding for urgency while his primary care physician considers a non-anticholinergic option. Increase donepezil from 5 mg to 10 mg nightly if his home heart rate stays at or above 55, since he is also on metoprolol. Hospital day 3 for a 63-year-old female admitted with sepsis from a urinary source due to E. coli pyelonephritis. Overnight she had no fever, rigors, or hypotension. She has current tobacco use of about half a pack of cigarettes per day and asked about help quitting.

Current medications are ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours since admission, acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed, and enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for VTE prophylaxis. IV fluids were stopped yesterday after her blood pressure normalized.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good morning. I have you down as a 63-year-old female here for follow-up of your breast cancer. How have you been doing on the anastrozole?
Patient: Overall okay, but my joints are so stiff. My hands and knees ache, especially in the morning, and it has gotten worse since I started it about eight months ago.
Doctor: How bad is the aching, and does it keep you from doing things?
Patient: About a five out of ten. It takes me half an hour to loosen up, and I have been walking less because of my knees.
Doctor: Any swelling or redness in the joints?
Patient: No swelling, no redness.
Doctor: Any hot flashes?
Patient: A few at night, nothing terrible.
Doctor: Any new lumps in the breast or armpit, or changes in the skin or nipple?
Patient: No lumps, no changes.
Doctor: Any bone pain, back pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, or vaginal bleeding?
Patient: No to all of those.
Doctor: What medicines are you taking?
Patient: Anastrozole 1 mg once a day, amlodipine 5 mg for my blood pressure, and Tylenol sometimes for the aches.
Doctor: Do you take calcium or vitamin D?
Patient: No, I don't.
Doctor: Okay. Your vitals today are blood pressure 134/82 and heart rate 76. On exam, both breasts and both armpits are free of masses, the scar from your surgery is well healed, and I feel no enlarged lymph nodes. The knuckles and both knees are mildly tender without swelling or warmth. Your mammogram last month was normal. The bone density scan you had last week shows a T-score of -2.7 at the hip, which is osteoporosis.
Patient: Is the cancer back?
Doctor: No. There is no sign of recurrence. You had an ER-positive breast cancer treated with lumpectomy and radiation 18 months ago, and the mammogram is clear. The joint aches are from the anastrozole, and the anastrozole can also thin the bones, which is why the scan shows osteoporosis.
Patient: What do we do about it?
Doctor: Continue the anastrozole once a day, because it lowers the chance of the cancer returning. Start alendronate 70 mg once a week, first thing in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, and stay upright for 30 minutes. Start vitamin D3 1000 units daily and calcium through food and a supplement to reach 1200 mg a day. You should see your dentist before the first alendronate dose. I will check a vitamin D level and a calcium level today. For the aches, you can take Tylenol 1000 mg up to three times a day, and I will send you to physical therapy for a strengthening program. We will repeat the bone density scan in 2 years, and I want to see you back in 3 months.
Patient: Okay, I understand. Thank you.
"""

reference: A 63-year-old female on adjuvant anastrozole for ER-positive breast cancer treated with lumpectomy and radiation 18 months ago reported worsening hand and knee aches and morning stiffness without swelling, redness, new lumps or bone pain. Exam showed no breast masses or lymphadenopathy and mild joint tenderness, mammogram was normal, and bone density showed a hip T-score of -2.7. The impression was no recurrence, anastrozole-related joint aches and osteoporosis. Anastrozole continues, alendronate 70 mg weekly and vitamin D3 were started, calcium was advised, Tylenol is allowed for aches, physical therapy was arranged, and follow-up is in 3 months.

"""
Psych ED consult.
75-year-old female c/o "feeling like I'm dying" x 1 hr, brought by ambulance (neighbor called 911).
HPI: abrupt onset palpitations, SOB, chest tightness, tingling in both hands, sweating, and fear of dying. Peaked at ~10 min, now resolving. 3rd episode this month, none this bad. Triggered while alone at home watching TV, no clear trigger. Worried about having another one.
Denies SI, HI, AVH. No syncope, no fever. No alcohol, no drug use. 2 cups coffee/day.
PMH: panic disorder dx 5 yrs ago, HTN, hypothyroidism. No hx of CAD.
Home meds: sertraline 25 mg daily, lorazepam 0.5 mg PRN (uses ~3x/wk), amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 50 mcg daily.
SH: lives alone, widowed, daughter calls daily. No tobacco.

Vitals on arrival: BP 148/88, HR 112, RR 22, Temp 98.4 F, SpO2 98% RA.
Repeat after 1 hr: HR 84, RR 16, BP 130/78.
Exam: anxious, tremulous, speaking fluently. Lungs CTA. RRR no m/r/g. No LE edema. Neuro nonfocal.
MSE: A&Ox3, cooperative, anxious affect, linear thought process, no psychosis, no SI/HI, insight good.

Data:
ECG sinus tachycardia 108, no ST changes, QTc normal.
Troponin neg x2.
BMP nl, K 4.1, glucose 104.
CBC: WBC 7.2, Hgb 13.0.
TSH 2.1.
CXR clear.

Impression: panic attack in pt w/ known panic disorder. Medically cleared: cardiac, pulmonary, thyroid causes unlikely. Lorazepam use is a fall risk at her age.

Plan:
- Increase sertraline 25 mg to 50 mg daily
- D/c lorazepam, no refill
- Cont amlodipine, levothyroxine
- Refer outpt psychiatry for CBT
- Breathing/relaxation techniques reviewed
- Cut caffeine
- F/u PCP 1 wk
- D/c home with daughter. Return for CP, syncope, SI
"""

Initial heart rate was 112, improving to 84, with ECG sinus tachycardia and negative troponin, BMP, CBC, TSH, and chest x-ray. The impression is a panic attack with known panic disorder, medically cleared. Sertraline is increased to 50 mg daily, lorazepam is discontinued, outpatient psychiatry referral for CBT is made, and she is discharged home with PCP follow-up in 1 week.

Clinical note:
"""
Dictating a dermatology clinic follow-up visit for a 25-year-old male with hidradenitis suppurativa. He is here because of worsening painful nodules in both armpits and in the groin, which he has had for about four years, and he says the flares now come every two to three weeks with drainage that stains his shirts. He rates the pain at seven out of ten during a flare. He denies fever, chills, weight loss, joint pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea, and he has had no hospital stays. He is a smoker, about half a pack a day.

He is very anxious today and asked me a lot of questions, so I will list them. He asked whether this is contagious and I told him it is not. He asked whether poor hygiene caused it and I told him no. He asked whether shaving or deodorant is to blame, whether his diet matters, whether it will scar, whether the biologic can cause cancer or serious infection, whether he can drink alcohol on treatment, and whether he will have this forever. I answered each one in plain language, went over the expected course, and gave him a written handout.

For current treatment, he tells me he takes doxycycline 50 mg twice daily, correction, that is 100 mg twice daily, which I confirmed from his pharmacy list, and he has been on it for about four months with only partial improvement. He uses clindamycin 1% topical solution once daily on the armpits and groin and washes with chlorhexidine in the shower. For pain he takes acetaminophen 500 mg every six hours as needed. He also takes over-the-counter supplements on his own, namely zinc gluconate 50 mg daily, turmeric capsules, and vitamin D3 2000 units daily, and he wanted to know if these are helping. He has no known drug allergies.

On examination, blood pressure 126/78, heart rate 84, temperature 98.6 F, weight 98 kilograms, body mass index 31. Skin examination shows multiple inflamed nodules, two draining sinus tracts, and scarring in the left axilla, with similar findings in the right axilla and both inguinal folds, consistent with Hurley stage two. There is one tender fluctuant abscess about 2 cm in the left axilla. There is no spreading redness and no enlarged lymph nodes. I performed an incision and drainage of the left axillary abscess under 1% lidocaine local anesthesia, with a moderate amount of pus released, and he tolerated it well despite his nervousness.

My impression is hidradenitis suppurativa, Hurley stage two, with an inadequate response to doxycycline and a left axillary abscess drained today. For the plan, I am stopping the doxycycline. I am increasing the clindamycin 1% solution to twice daily. I ordered QuantiFERON, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, a complete blood count, and a comprehensive metabolic panel, and once these return normal I will start adalimumab, 160 mg subcutaneously on day one, 80 mg on day fifteen, then 40 mg weekly. He will continue the chlorhexidine wash and acetaminophen as needed. I told him the evidence for turmeric is weak, but he may continue zinc gluconate and vitamin D3 if he wishes. I counseled him on smoking cessation and weight loss and placed a dietitian referral. Injection teaching will be done by our nurse. He should return in four weeks, or sooner for fever, spreading redness, or a new painful lump that does not drain. End of dictation.
"""

"""
Dictating a dermatology clinic follow-up visit for a 25-year-old male with hidradenitis suppurativa. He is here because of worsening painful nodules in both armpits and in the groin, which he has had for about four years, and he says the flares now come every two to three weeks with drainage that stains his shirts. He rates the pain at seven out of ten during a flare. He denies fever, chills, weight loss, joint pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea, and he has had no hospital stays. He is a smoker, about half a pack a day.

He is very anxious today and asked me a lot of questions, so I will list them. He asked whether this is contagious and I told him it is not. He asked whether poor hygiene caused it and I told him no. He asked whether shaving or deodorant is to blame, whether his diet matters, whether it will scar, whether the biologic can cause cancer or serious infection, whether he can drink alcohol on treatment, and whether he will have this forever. I answered each one in plain language, went over the expected course, and gave him a written handout.

For current treatment, he tells me he takes doxycycline 50 mg twice daily, correction, that is 100 mg twice daily, which I confirmed from his pharmacy list, and he has been on it for about four months with only partial improvement. He uses clindamycin 1% topical solution once daily on the armpits and groin and washes with chlorhexidine in the shower. For pain he takes acetaminophen 500 mg every six hours as needed. He also takes over-the-counter supplements on his own, namely zinc gluconate 50 mg daily, turmeric capsules, and vitamin D3 2000 units daily, and he wanted to know if these are helping. There is one tender fluctuant abscess about 2 cm in the left axilla. There is no spreading redness and no enlarged lymph nodes. I performed an incision and drainage of the left axillary abscess under 1% lidocaine local anesthesia, with a moderate amount of pus released, and he tolerated it well despite his nervousness.

My impression is hidradenitis suppurativa, Hurley stage two, with an inadequate response to doxycycline and a left axillary abscess drained today. For the plan, I am stopping the doxycycline. I am increasing the clindamycin 1% solution to twice daily. I ordered QuantiFERON, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, a complete blood count, and a comprehensive metabolic panel, and once these return normal I will start adalimumab, 160 mg subcutaneously on day one, 80 mg on day fifteen, then 40 mg weekly. He will continue the chlorhexidine wash and acetaminophen as needed. I told him the evidence for turmeric is weak, but he may continue zinc gluconate and vitamin D3 if he wishes. """
1-year-old female brought to urgent care by dad.
CC: cough and runny nose x4 d, fever x2 d, breathing fast today.
Dad first said fever x4 d, then clarified: fever x2 d, cough/rhinorrhea x4 d. Final = fever x2 d.
Feeding ~50% of usual volume last 24 hr, 3 wet diapers today (usually 5-6).
Wheeze per dad, worse overnight. Sibling at daycare w/ URI.
Denies vomiting, diarrhea, apnea, cyanosis, stridor, rash.
Dad stopped OTC cough syrup (dextromethorphan) tonight after reading the label.
PMH: ex-34 wk preemie (no NICU oxygen), eczema, GERD, iron deficiency anemia (Hgb 10.9 at routine screen).
Meds per dad: famotidine 10 mg BID. Bottle checked in clinic, dad corrected: famotidine 5 mg BID. Also hydrocortisone 1% cream BID to eczema patches, ferrous sulfate 15 mg daily, vitamin D 400 IU daily, acetaminophen 120 mg q6h PRN fever (last dose 4 hr ago).
NKDA. Imms UTD. Did not receive RSV monoclonal antibody last fall per dad. No prior hospitalizations or ED visits for breathing problems. No smoke exposure at home. Mom is home w/ pt and sibling, dad works nights.
Vitals: Temp 100.4 F, HR 148, RR 52, SpO2 94% RA (95% after suctioning), wt 10 kg.
Exam: alert, fussy but consolable, MMM, cap refill <2 sec.
Nares w/ clear rhinorrhea, TMs clear bilat. Throat mildly erythematous, no exudate.
Heart tachycardic but regular, no murmur.
Mild nasal flaring, mild subcostal retractions.
Diffuse expiratory wheeze, scattered crackles.
No grunting.
Abd soft NT/ND.
Skin: eczema patches on cheeks and extensor arms.
Nasal suctioning done w/ improvement in congestion and work of breathing.
Trial of albuterol neb 2.5 mg x1: no change in RR or retractions, so d/c'd, not indicated for bronchiolitis.
RSV PCR positive. CXR not obtained, no focal findings and SpO2 >92%.
Observed 1 hr after suction: RR 44, SpO2 96% RA, took 3 oz formula w/o difficulty.
A/P:
Bronchiolitis (RSV), mild-moderate, hydration adequate, safe for home.
Supportive care: nasal saline + bulb suction before feeds, small frequent feeds, offer fluids often.
Acetaminophen dose was low for wt: change to 150 mg (4.7 mL of 160 mg/5 mL) q6h PRN.
No albuterol at home. STOP dextromethorphan cough syrup, not for young children.
Continue famotidine 5 mg BID, hydrocortisone 1% cream BID, ferrous sulfate 15 mg daily, vitamin D 400 IU daily.
ED now if RR >60, worse retractions, apnea, color change, or <3 wet diapers in 24 hr.
Discussed expected course w/ dad: cough can last 2-3 wks, worst around days 3-5 of illness, so symptoms may look worse before better.
Dad verbalized understanding, teach-back done.
PCP recheck in 24-48 hr.
"""

Physical therapy evaluation and ambulation with fall precautions; he was instructed to rise slowly. Repeat BMP in the morning. She has a history of migraine without aura and takes no regular medications other than an oral contraceptive.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Hello. I understand you are a 25-year-old female with Graves disease, and you came in today because of a racing heart. Is this your mother with you?
Family member: Yes, I'm her mother. I came along because she has been getting worse for the past two weeks.
Doctor: Tell me what has been going on.
Patient: My heart is pounding all the time, my hands shake, and I'm sweating even when it's cold. I'm so tired, but I can't sleep.
Family member: She has lost weight too, about 12 pounds in a month, and she has been very irritable. I also noticed she ran out of her methimazole about three weeks ago and did not get a refill for a while.
Patient: Yes, I ran out. I was taking 10 milligrams once a day before that.
Doctor: Any chest pain, trouble breathing, vomiting, fever, or confusion?
Patient: No chest pain and no trouble breathing. No vomiting and no fever.
Family member: No confusion either. She is thinking clearly, just anxious.
Doctor: Any sore throat? That matters with this medicine.
Patient: No sore throat.
Doctor: Any eye problems, like double vision or eye pain?
Patient: My eyes feel a bit dry and gritty, but no double vision and no eye pain.
Doctor: Could you be pregnant?
Patient: No, I had my period last week.
Doctor: Okay. Today your heart rate is 118, blood pressure 134/72, temperature 99.1, and respiratory rate 18. You have a fine tremor of the outstretched hands, warm moist skin, and a diffusely enlarged thyroid without nodules. Your reflexes are brisk. Your eyes show mild lid retraction but normal eye movements. The heart is fast but regular and the lungs are clear. The blood work shows a TSH of less than 0.01 and a free T4 of 3.4, which is high. The urine pregnancy test is negative, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia and nothing else.
Family member: Is it dangerous?
Doctor: It is not thyroid storm, because she is alert, her temperature is only slightly up, and there is no vomiting. But it is uncontrolled Graves disease from missing the methimazole. I am restarting methimazole at a higher dose, 20 mg once daily, and starting propranolol 20 mg three times a day to slow the heart and control the tremor.
Patient: Anything I should watch for?
Doctor: Yes. Methimazole can rarely drop the white blood cells, so if you get a fever or sore throat, stop it and call us right away. I am sending a CBC with differential and liver tests today as a baseline. It can also harm a pregnancy, so please use reliable birth control. You will see endocrinology within 1 week, and we will repeat the thyroid labs in 4 weeks. Go to the emergency department for chest pain, fainting, vomiting, or confusion.
Family member: We understand. Thank you.
"""

She denied chest pain, trouble breathing, vomiting, fever, confusion, and sore throat. Her heart rate was 118, TSH was suppressed, free T4 was high, and the ECG showed sinus tachycardia. The assessment was uncontrolled Graves disease without thyroid storm. Methimazole was restarted at 20 mg once daily, propranolol was started, baseline blood work was ordered, and endocrinology follow-up was arranged within 1 week.

Clinical note:
"""
Ambient scribe transcript. Gastroenterology specialty clinic follow-up visit for a 66-year-old female with celiac disease.

Doctor: Good to see you. It has been about a year since your celiac diagnosis. How are you feeling?
Patient: Better than before, but I still get bloated after meals sometimes, and I'm tired a lot.
Doctor: Any diarrhea, belly pain, or weight loss?
Patient: No diarrhea, no belly pain, and my weight has been steady.
Doctor: Any black stools or blood in your stool, since you take a blood thinner?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: How strict have you been with the gluten-free diet?
Patient: Pretty strict at home. When we eat out I'm not always sure, so I probably get some cross-contact.
Doctor: That's common. What medicines are you taking?
Patient: Apixaban 5 mg twice a day for my atrial fibrillation, ferrous sulfate 325 mg every day, and a vitamin D supplement.
Doctor: Any trouble with the iron?
Patient: It gives me constipation.
Doctor: Your vitals today are blood pressure 126/74, heart rate 72 and a bit irregular, and oxygen saturation 98 percent. Patient: So is the celiac still active?
Doctor: It means some gluten is still getting in, and the low ferritin tells us your iron stores are still low. My impression is celiac disease with ongoing mild gluten exposure, iron-deficiency anemia, and your atrial fibrillation is stable on the apixaban. For the iron, let's change the ferrous sulfate to 325 mg every other day, which absorbs better and is easier on the bowels. Continue the apixaban and the vitamin D. I want you to meet with our dietitian about eating out safely. I'll order a repeat upper endoscopy with small bowel biopsies, and we'll coordinate with your cardiologist about holding the apixaban for a short time before the procedure. Come back in 3 months.
Patient: Okay, that sounds good.
"""

The patient is a 52-year-old female seen in orthopedic clinic for follow-up of low back pain that radiates down the left leg. The pain began about five weeks ago after she lifted a heavy box and now runs from the left buttock to the outer calf and the top of the left foot. It is 7 out of 10 when sitting or coughing and eases when she stands or walks. She has numbness over the top of the left foot and has noticed her left big toe catching when she walks. She denies bowel or bladder dysfunction, saddle numbness, fever, weight loss, and any fall or other injury. She has hypertension and GERD. Her medications are lisinopril 10 mg daily and omeprazole 20 mg daily, plus over-the-counter naproxen 500 mg BID that has helped only partly and has caused epigastric burning for the past week.

Straight leg raise is positive on the left at 40 degrees and negative on the right. Left great toe extension strength is 4/5, other muscle groups are 5/5, and sensation is decreased over the dorsum of the left foot. Patellar and Achilles reflexes are 2+ and symmetric.

I reviewed the MRI of the lumbar spine obtained two weeks ago, which shows an L4-L5 left paracentral disc protrusion contacting the traversing left L5 nerve root, with mild foraminal narrowing and no compression of the cauda equina.

My impression is left L5 radiculopathy from an L4-L5 disc herniation with a mild motor deficit. Her hypertension is controlled, and her GERD symptoms are aggravated by the naproxen. I advised her to stop naproxen and started prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days, and we discussed checking her home blood pressure during the course. I also started gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime. She will continue lisinopril and omeprazole. I referred her to physical therapy and encouraged her to stay active rather than rest in bed. If there is no improvement in 4 to 6 weeks, we will discuss an epidural steroid injection, and she was told to go to the emergency department immediately for new leg weakness, numbness in the groin, or loss of bladder or bowel control. Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good morning, thanks for coming in. Before we start, let me confirm: you are a 41-year-old female, six weeks out from your cesarean delivery, right?
Patient: Yes, that's right. Baby girl, and she's doing great.
Doctor: Wonderful. How have you been feeling yourself?
Patient: Tired, mostly. The baby is up every two or three hours and I'm breastfeeding, so it's a lot. But no big problems.
Doctor: Tell me about the incision.
Patient: It's a little sore when I bend over, but it isn't red and nothing is leaking.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No, none.
Doctor: And your bleeding?
Patient: It's light now, just some spotting. It was heavy the first couple of weeks.
Doctor: Any calf pain or calf swelling? Any chest pain or trouble breathing?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: How is your mood? A lot of women feel very low after delivery.
Patient: I get weepy sometimes, but I'm not down all the time. I try to sleep when the baby sleeps.
Doctor: You filled out the Edinburgh questionnaire in the waiting room and your score was 6, which is reassuring.
Patient: Okay, good.
Doctor: I see you had high blood pressure at the end of the pregnancy and went home on labetalol 100 mg twice a day. Are you still taking it?
Patient: Yes, twice a day. I check at home and it's usually around 115 over 75.
Doctor: Today it's 118 over 76 with a heart rate of 74. Your hemoglobin at discharge was 9.6, so we rechecked it this morning. It's 10.8, still a bit low. Have you been taking any iron?
Patient: No, nobody told me to.
Doctor: Okay. I'll start ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day. Take it with orange juice, not with your coffee, and it can make you constipated.
Patient: Alright. What about birth control? I definitely don't want another baby.
Doctor: Since you're breastfeeding, I'd avoid pills with estrogen. A levonorgestrel IUD is a great option, and I can place it at your next visit in two weeks. Until then, use condoms.
Patient: Okay, that works.
Doctor: On exam, your incision is clean, dry and well healed, your uterus is firm and back down in the pelvis, your lungs are clear, and your legs aren't swollen.
Doctor: So, you're recovering well from your cesarean delivery. Your blood pressure is normal now, so you can stop the labetalol. Keep checking at home for two more weeks and call me if it goes above 140 over 90. You have mild anemia, so start the iron, and we'll recheck your blood count in six weeks. Your mood screen is normal, but call us if the weepiness gets worse. Come back in two weeks for the IUD.
Patient: Thank you.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Hi, I'm the emergency doctor. I hear your lips are swelling. You're a 29-year-old male, right?
Patient: Yes. About an hour ago I ate dinner at a seafood place, shrimp pasta, and my lips started tingling and then swelling. Now my tongue feels thick and I have itchy bumps on my chest and arms.
Doctor: Any trouble breathing, wheezing, or a tight throat?
Patient: No, I can breathe okay, but my voice sounds a little funny.
Doctor: Any vomiting, belly pain, or lightheadedness?
Patient: No, none of that.
Doctor: Have you ever reacted to shrimp or other shellfish before?
Patient: Never. I've eaten shrimp lots of times. And I don't take any regular medicines.
Doctor: Okay. Nurse, can you read me the vitals?
Nurse: Blood pressure 128 over 78, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 98.4.
Doctor: Thanks. On exam your upper and lower lips are visibly swollen, your tongue is mildly enlarged, but your uvula looks normal and your airway is open. You have hives on your chest and arms. Your lungs are clear with no wheezing.
Doctor: This is an allergic reaction with angioedema, most likely from shellfish. I'm giving you epinephrine 0.3 mg into the thigh muscle right now, and diphenhydramine 50 mg through the IV. We'll watch you closely on the monitor for at least four hours.
Patient: Okay. Should I be worried?
Doctor: Your airway is open right now and these medicines work quickly. If your breathing changes, tell the nurse right away.
Nurse: The swelling is already improving after the epinephrine.
Doctor: Good. If you stay stable, you can go home with an epinephrine auto-injector, 0.3 mg, and I'm referring you to an allergist for testing. Avoid all shellfish until then.
Patient: Understood. Thank you.
"""

- Neuro: DTRs 2+, no clonus

- Continue ibuprofen PRN, docusate, prenatal vitamin

c/o: feels tired but ok. Perineal soreness, improving.
- Denies headache, visual changes, RUQ pain, SOB, chest pain, calf pain or swelling, fever, heavy bleeding
- Lochia scant, no clots, no foul odor
- Breastfeeding, baby feeding well
- Mood: tired, EPDS 6, denies low mood
- Home BPs not checked, no cuff

PMH: gestational HTN this pregnancy only. NKDA.

Meds:
- nifedipine ER 30 mg daily
- ibuprofen 600 mg q6h PRN perineal pain
- docusate 100 mg BID
- prenatal vitamin daily

Vitals: BP 148/92, recheck 144/90 after 10 min rest, HR 84, Temp 98.4 F, RR 16, SpO2 99% RA

Exam:
- NAD, lungs CTAB, heart RRR
- Abd soft, fundus firm, nontender
- Perineum: 2nd degree laceration healing, edges approximated, no erythema or discharge
- Legs: no edema, no calf tenderness
- Neuro: DTRs 2+, no clonus

Data: UA dip trace protein, neg leuk, neg nitrite. POC Hgb 10.8.

Impression:
1. Postpartum day 12, recovering well
2. Gestational HTN, mild-range BPs on nifedipine, no severe features (no headache, no visual sx, no RUQ pain, trace protein only)
3. Perineal laceration, healing
4. Mild postpartum anemia

Rx/f/u:
- Increase nifedipine ER 30 mg -> 60 mg daily
- Continue ibuprofen PRN, docusate, prenatal vitamin
- Labs today: CBC, CMP, urine protein/creatinine ratio; will call pt w/ results
- Home BP checks BID w/ log (cuff given); call OB if >= 150/100; ED if >= 160/110 or headache, vision change, RUQ pain, SOB
- OB visit in 1 wk for BP recheck, comprehensive postpartum visit at 6 wk
- Contraception: pt interested in implant, discuss at OB visit
- Nifedipine OK w/ breastfeeding

Clinical note:
"""
Dictating a follow-up visit in the oncology clinic. The patient is a 38-year-old male with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma, never smoker, PD-L1 expression 80 percent, no actionable driver mutation, on pembrolizumab 200 mg IV every 3 weeks. Today is cycle five, correction, cycle six. His wife attends today and provides part of the history because he tends to minimize his symptoms.

Per the patient he feels more tired over the past 3 weeks, and he is cold all the time even when others are comfortable. His wife adds that he has been sleeping about 12 hours a night, has gained some weight, and has had constipation, which is new. He reports a mild dry cough that is unchanged since starting treatment. He denies fever, shortness of breath, chest pain, diarrhea, abdominal pain, rash, and headache. His wife agrees that he has had no vomiting or blood in the stool. Appetite is good. His only other medication is acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for mild back discomfort, which he rarely uses.

Vital signs today: blood pressure 122/76, heart rate 56, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air, temperature 98.2 F. Weight is up 3 kg from the last cycle. On exam he is in no distress and ECOG performance status is 1. His skin is dry. The thyroid is not enlarged or tender. Lungs are clear with no wheeze. Abdomen is soft and nontender. No peripheral edema.

Data. TSH is elevated at 14.2, free T4 is low at 0.6, and his baseline TSH before starting immunotherapy was 2.1. White count 6.8, hemoglobin 12.9, creatinine 0.9, ALT 31. Restaging CT chest last week showed a partial response of the primary tumor and no new lesions.

Assessment. One, stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with partial response on pembrolizumab. Two, immune-related hypothyroidism, which explains the fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, and low heart rate. Three, mild dry cough, stable, with no signs of pneumonitis.

Plan. Proceed with pembrolizumab cycle six today. Start levothyroxine 50 mcg daily on an empty stomach, and I reviewed this with both the patient and his wife. Repeat TSH and free T4 in 6 weeks. Wife counseled to call for new shortness of breath, diarrhea, or severe fatigue. Return in 3 weeks for the next cycle.
"""

Cycle six of pembrolizumab proceeds, levothyroxine 50 mcg daily was started, TSH and free T4 will be rechecked in 6 weeks, and he returns in 3 weeks.

Clinical note:
"""
This is a dictation for a gastroenterology inpatient progress note on hospital day 3. The patient is a 53-year-old female with ulcerative colitis admitted with a flare, and I am dictating after seeing her on the ward and speaking with the pharmacist and the social worker.

Interval history. She was admitted three days ago with about ten bloody stools a day, correction, eight bloody stools a day, along with abdominal cramping, urgency, and nocturnal stools for two weeks. Overnight she had four bloody stools, down from six the night before, and she says the cramping is better. She had mild fatigue and a low-grade fever on admission, and the fever has resolved. She denies vomiting, severe abdominal pain, and shortness of breath.

Medication history and cost. On admission she told the team she had stopped her mesalamine altogether six weeks ago because the copay went up after her insurance changed. On further questioning today she clarified, correction, that she did not stop it. She has been taking 2.4 g once daily, half of the prescribed 4.8 g once daily, by cutting her tablets to stretch the supply. She has also been taking over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg as needed for joint pain several times a week. Her other history includes hypertension, hypothyroidism, gastroesophageal reflux, and osteopenia. Her other home medications are levothyroxine 88 mcg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. She has no known drug allergies.

Inpatient medications so far are IV methylprednisolone 40 mg every 12 hours since admission, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for prophylaxis, and one dose of potassium chloride 40 mEq by mouth yesterday for low potassium.

Vitals this morning are temperature 98.6, blood pressure 128/76, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. She looks tired but not toxic. The abdomen is soft with mild left lower quadrant tenderness, no distension, no rebound, and no guarding, and bowel sounds are present. There is no peripheral edema, no oral ulcers, and no joint effusions.

Data. Hemoglobin 10.2, white count 11.8, platelets 410, albumin 2.9, CRP 48 mg/L, potassium 3.4 on admission and 3.9 after repletion, and creatinine 0.8. Stool C. difficile PCR and stool cultures are negative. Abdominal x-ray shows no colonic dilation and no free air. Flexible sigmoidoscopy has not been done yet.

Assessment and plan. She has a moderate to severe ulcerative colitis flare, precipitated by under-dosing of mesalamine because of cost and by NSAID use, and it is responding to IV steroids. She also has anemia and hypokalemia, which is improving, and her hypertension and hypothyroidism are stable. Today I am switching IV methylprednisolone to oral prednisone 40 mg daily. I am increasing mesalamine back to the full 4.8 g once daily. I am stopping ibuprofen and she is to avoid all NSAIDs, using acetaminophen for joint pain instead. Continue levothyroxine, lisinopril, omeprazole, and enoxaparin. Repeat CBC and basic metabolic panel in the morning. Flexible sigmoidoscopy tomorrow to assess severity before deciding on a biologic, with hepatitis B serologies and QuantiFERON sent today in case a biologic is needed. The social worker and pharmacist will help her apply for a manufacturer assistance program and will find a lower cost mesalamine formulation. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation given steroid exposure and osteopenia. If she continues to improve she may go home in two days, with gastroenterology clinic follow-up in two weeks. That completes the dictation.
"""

She first said she had stopped mesalamine but clarified she was taking half the prescribed dose because of cost, and she also used ibuprofen. Hemoglobin was 10.2 and CRP 48 mg/L, infectious stool studies were negative, and abdominal x-ray showed no colonic dilation. IV methylprednisolone was changed to prednisone 40 mg daily, mesalamine was increased to 4.8 g once daily, and ibuprofen was stopped. Flexible sigmoidoscopy, pre-biologic screening, cost-assistance referrals, and clinic follow-up in two weeks were planned.

"""
Nephrology consultation. Requesting service is hospital medicine. Reason for consult is volume overload in a patient on maintenance hemodialysis.

HPI: This is a 65-year-old male with end-stage renal disease from diabetic nephropathy on in-center hemodialysis three times weekly through a left arm arteriovenous fistula. He was admitted last night with shortness of breath and leg swelling. He returned about ten days ago from a three-week trip abroad, during which he completed only two dialysis sessions, and he admits to eating salty restaurant meals and drinking more fluids than usual. He estimates he has gained about 6 kg above his dry weight. He reports orthopnea and ankle swelling. He denies chest pain, fever, diarrhea, and cough. He still makes a small amount of urine.

Past history: end-stage renal disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. Home medications are amlodipine 10 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and sevelamer carbonate 800 mg three times daily with meals. No known drug allergies.

Data: potassium 5.8, sodium 134, hemoglobin 9.6. Chest x-ray shows pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral pleural effusions. ECG shows sinus rhythm without peaked T waves. Hepatitis B surface antigen was negative at the dialysis unit last month.

Impression: Volume overload from missed dialysis sessions and dietary sodium and fluid excess in end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis. Mild hyperkalemia. Hypertension, likely volume-mediated.

Recommendations: Urgent hemodialysis tonight with an ultrafiltration goal of 3 to 4 liters as tolerated and a 2 potassium bath. Daily dialysis until he reaches his dry weight. Strict intake and output, a low-salt diet, and a fluid restriction of 1 liter per day. Repeat BMP after dialysis. Supplemental oxygen to keep saturation above 92%. Given the recent international travel, recheck hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody per dialysis unit protocol and notify his outpatient unit before he returns. Social work to help arrange dialysis for future travel. We will follow daily.
"""

The patient is a 23-year-old male seen in the dermatology clinic for follow-up of acne vulgaris that began in his mid-teens. He reports inflammatory papules and pustules across the cheeks, forehead, and jawline, with occasional painful nodules along the left jawline that leave dark marks when they resolve. Over the past 6 months he has used an over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide 5% wash once daily with only partial improvement. He denies itching or burning of the skin, denies fever, and denies any previous prescription acne treatment. He has no other medical conditions, takes no other medications, and has no known drug allergies. He is a university student, does not smoke, and has not noticed worsening with particular foods.

On examination he is well appearing. There are scattered inflammatory papules and pustules across both cheeks and the forehead, comedones on the nose and chin, and three tender nodules along the left jawline. There is mild post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation but no ice-pick scarring, and the chest and back are clear.

My impression is moderate inflammatory acne vulgaris with a partial response to benzoyl peroxide alone. I am starting tretinoin 0.025% cream, to be applied to the face every night at bedtime, and he will continue the benzoyl peroxide wash each morning. I counseled him on sun protection, using a non-comedogenic moisturizer, and the expected early dryness and irritation. He will return in 12 weeks to reassess his response, and we will discuss other options at that visit if improvement is inadequate.
"""

- asthma, mild persistent -- stable, no ED visits this yr, no night sx
- allergic rhinitis
- eczema, mild
NKDA.

- fluticasone HFA 110 mcg 1 puff BID
- albuterol HFA 90 mcg 2 puffs q4-6h PRN, uses ~1x/wk
- cetirizine 5 mg daily
- montelukast 5 mg qHS -- stopped by mom 2 mo ago b/c nightmares, not restarted
No other OTC meds.

VS: T 101.1 F, HR 98, RR 18, BP 108/66, SpO2 99% RA.
Wt 38 kg -- correction, 41 kg on repeat (shoes on first reading).

- non-toxic, NAD

- tender anterior cervical LAD bilat
- no trismus, no peritonsillar bulge, no muffled voice
- lungs CTAB, no wheeze
- no rash
- abd soft NT

McIsaac score 5

1. Strep pharyngitis (GAS), RADT +
- amoxicillin 1000 mg PO once daily x 10 d, taken w/ breakfast; once-daily dosing chosen b/c of mom's irregular shifts
- ibuprofen 400 mg PO q8h PRN pain/fever w/ food, max 3 doses/day
- salt water gargles, cold fluids, soft diet
- school note, back to school after 24 h of abx + afebrile
- replace toothbrush after 48 h of abx
- mom + grandparent both taught dosing, phone alarm set for 8 AM, teach-back done
- f/u by phone/video in 3 d b/c mom cannot make clinic visits around shifts, sooner if worse; no test of cure
2. Asthma, mild persistent
- continue fluticasone HFA 110 mcg 1 puff BID + albuterol HFA PRN
- montelukast stays OFF, nightmares added to chart as adverse reaction
3. Allergic rhinitis
- increase cetirizine from 5 mg to 10 mg daily
4. Eczema, mild
- continue daily moisturizer
- close contacts w/ sx should be seen
"""

Dermatology follow-up on the hospital ward for a 27-year-old male who is hospitalized for an unrelated orthopedic problem and asked for help with his facial skin. He has used an over-the-counter face wash intermittently without lasting benefit. He denies fever, denies itching, and denies any drainage from the lesions. He has no other chronic medical conditions and is not using any acne treatment at this time.

On examination he is comfortable and afebrile. There are multiple open and closed comedones across the forehead and cheeks, along with scattered inflammatory papules and a few pustules on the cheeks and jawline. I explained that this is unrelated to his hospital stay and that treatment takes eight to twelve weeks to show its full effect. I started adapalene 0.1% gel to be applied to the face every night at bedtime and benzoyl peroxide 5% gel to be applied each morning. He was advised to use a gentle cleanser and a non-comedogenic moisturizer, to avoid picking at the lesions, and to expect some dryness during the first two weeks. He will follow up in dermatology clinic eight weeks after discharge, and an oral antibiotic can be considered if the response is inadequate.
"""

Doctor: How does it compare with your usual crises?
Patient: About the same, maybe a little worse. I work nights in a hotel kitchen and some weeks they switch me to days, so I've barely slept and I haven't been drinking much water. I felt warm last night.

"""
Hospital day 3 progress note for a 64-year-old female admitted with acute decompensated heart failure.

Interval events: There were no rapid response calls and no arrhythmia on telemetry overnight. She slept propped up on two pillows, down from three pillows at home, and says her breathing is better but she is still short of breath when walking to the bathroom. She was anxious this morning and asked many questions, including whether she will need a pacemaker, why her weight matters so much, and whether she can ever eat out again. Each question was answered and we reviewed the plan together. Her daughter, who lives with her and is her main caregiver, was at the bedside and provided part of the history. The daughter reports that over the past week the patient gained about 8 pounds, had worsening leg swelling, woke at night gasping for air, and was taking over-the-counter ibuprofen for knee pain up to three times daily. The patient denies chest pain, fever, productive cough, palpitations, and syncope.

Past medical history: HFrEF due to ischemic cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, CKD stage 3, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. No known drug allergies.

Medication reconciliation was clarified today. The daughter first said the patient takes carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, but when she brought in the pill bottles the label read 12.5 mg twice daily, so the correct home dose is carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily. Other home medications are spironolactone 25 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and metformin 500 mg twice daily. In the hospital, furosemide IV was increased this morning from 40 mg to 80 mg twice daily because she was net negative only 600 mL over the last 24 hours. Carvedilol, spironolactone, apixaban, and atorvastatin are continued. Ibuprofen has been discontinued and should not be restarted. Metformin is on hold, and she receives insulin lispro sliding scale. She was also given potassium chloride 40 mEq by mouth for hypokalemia.

Vitals this morning: temp 98.2 F, HR 78, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 95% on 2 L nasal cannula. Weight is 78.4 kg, down from 82.1 kg on admission.

Exam: She is anxious but comfortable at rest. JVP is elevated at about 10 cm, there are bibasilar crackles, and her rhythm is irregularly irregular with a 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex. She has 2+ pitting edema to the knees, her abdomen is soft, and her extremities are warm.

Data: BNP was 1450 on admission and troponin was negative twice. Today creatinine is 1.5 (baseline 1.3), K 3.4, Na 134, glucose 156, and Hgb 11.8. Chest X-ray shows pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral pleural effusions, improved from admission. Echo this admission showed an EF of 30%, down from 35% previously, with moderate mitral regurgitation. EKG shows atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular rate.

Assessment and plan:
1. Acute decompensated HFrEF, likely precipitated by NSAID use and dietary sodium. Continue furosemide 80 mg IV twice daily, daily weights, strict intake and output, a 2 g sodium diet, and fluid restriction of 1.5 L daily. Repeat BMP this afternoon. Expect to transition to an oral diuretic in 24 to 48 hours.
2. Mild creatinine rise above baseline, likely cardiorenal. Monitor with daily BMP and avoid nephrotoxins.
3. Hypokalemia. Potassium chloride given as above; recheck BMP this afternoon.
4. Atrial fibrillation, rate controlled. Continue carvedilol and apixaban at current doses.
5. Type 2 diabetes. Metformin held; continue sliding scale insulin.
6. Anxiety related to hospitalization. Reassurance given, questions answered, and written heart failure education provided to the patient and her daughter.
Disposition: Anticipate discharge in 3 to 4 days with heart failure clinic follow-up within 7 days of discharge and social work referral for a home scale.
"""

Clinical note:

Doctor: Hello, I'm the emergency physician. I understand you're an 84-year-old male with chest pain. Tell me what happened.
Patient: It started about two hours ago while I was watching television. It's a pressure right in the middle of my chest. Is this a heart attack? Should I be scared?
Doctor: We are going to find out, and we are moving quickly. Does the pain travel anywhere, like your arm or your jaw?
Patient: A little bit down my left arm. What tests are you going to do? Will they hurt?
Doctor: Just a blood draw and an ECG, nothing painful. Have you had any shortness of breath, nausea, or vomiting?
Patient: No shortness of breath and no vomiting. I felt a little sweaty when it started. Why would I be sweaty?
Doctor: That can happen with heart pain. Any cough, fever, or leg swelling?
Patient: No cough, no fever, and no swelling in my legs.
Doctor: What medical conditions do you have?
Patient: High blood pressure and high cholesterol, and I had a stent placed in my heart about six years ago. Does that matter?
Doctor: It matters a lot, thank you for telling me. What medicines do you take?
Patient: Aspirin 81 milligrams every morning, atorvastatin 40 milligrams at night, and lisinopril 20 milligrams in the morning. I took my aspirin today already. Is that okay?
Doctor: Yes, that's good. Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: None that I know of.

I am giving you nitroglycerin 0.4 mg under your tongue now, and I want to increase your atorvastatin from 40 mg to 80 mg nightly. We will also get a chest x-ray, call the cardiologist, and admit you to the hospital on a heart monitor. If the repeat troponin stays negative, you will likely have a stress test tomorrow.
Patient: How long will I be here? Can someone call my doctor?
Doctor: Probably overnight, and yes, we will let your primary doctor know.
"""

Doctor: Hello, I'm glad you both could come in. So you're a 71-year-old female, and your daughter came along because of some memory trouble?
Family member: Yes. Over the past year Mom keeps repeating the same questions, and last week she left the stove on twice.
Patient: I think everyone is making a fuss. I just misplace things, like my keys and my glasses.
Doctor: Has this been getting worse?
Family member: It was subtle at first, but it is clearly worse in the last three months. She forgot a doctor's appointment and she's been missing words.
Patient: Words are on the tip of my tongue sometimes.
Doctor: Any trouble finding your way around, like getting lost while driving or walking?
Patient: No, I still drive to the store with no problem.
Doctor: Any headaches, falls, weakness on one side, or hallucinations?

Doctor: What other medicines do you take, and do you have any allergies?

Doctor: My impression is mild cognitive impairment, and it may be early dementia. Your hypertension and hypothyroidism are stable, but the diphenhydramine is a known cause of memory problems in older adults, so I'd like you to stop it. I'm ordering an MRI of the brain without contrast and blood tests for B12, TSH, and a metabolic panel, plus a urinalysis to rule out infection. I'm also referring you to the neurology memory clinic for neuropsychological testing. Your daughter should check on the stove, and please don't drive far until we've reviewed the results. Patient: All right, I'll try that.
Family member: Thank you. We'll make sure she follows up.
"""
