Clinical note:
"""
Ambient scribe transcript. Gastroenterology outpatient clinic, evaluation of anemia in a 20-year-old female.

Doctor: Your primary care doctor sent you because your blood count showed low iron. What have you noticed?
Patient: I've been exhausted for months, and I get dizzy when I stand up fast. My friends say I look pale. I also keep craving ice, which sounds weird.
Doctor: How does your work schedule fit into this?
Patient: I work nights at a distribution center, three or four nights a week, but the schedule changes every week and sometimes they switch me to days. My sleep and my meals are all over the place.
Doctor: Any black or bloody stools?
Patient: No, never.
Doctor: Belly pain, diarrhea, or trouble swallowing?
Patient: No belly pain, no diarrhea, and swallowing is fine.
Doctor: Any weight loss?
Patient: No, my weight is the same.
Doctor: Tell me about your periods.
Patient: They are heavy. They last about seven days, and I soak a pad every two or three hours on the first two days, with some clots.
Doctor: What are you taking?
Patient: Ferrous sulfate 325 mg twice a day, omeprazole 20 mg every morning that I bought over the counter for heartburn, ibuprofen 400 mg when I get a migraine, sertraline 100 mg daily, and my albuterol inhaler for asthma.
Doctor: Let's go through the iron again. Twice a day?
Patient: Sorry, no. I only take the iron once a day, and I skip it on nights when I am rushing to work.
Doctor: And the sertraline? My list shows 50 mg.
Patient: Let me look at the bottle. You are right, it is 50 mg once a day.
Doctor: Thank you. Your vital signs today are blood pressure 104/62, heart rate 96, and oxygen saturation 99 percent. You look pale and your conjunctivae are pale. Your heart rhythm is regular with a soft flow murmur, your lungs are clear, and your abdomen is soft and not tender, with no liver or spleen enlargement. Your labs from last week show a hemoglobin of 9.1, an MCV of 74, and a ferritin of 6, which confirms iron deficiency. The celiac antibody, tissue transglutaminase IgA, was negative with a normal total IgA, and your pregnancy test was negative.
Patient: So what is causing it?
Doctor: My impression is iron-deficiency anemia, most likely from your heavy periods, but we also need to rule out a bleeding or absorption problem in the gut. The omeprazole and the ibuprofen can both make this worse, since the acid blocker reduces iron absorption and ibuprofen can irritate the stomach and cause bleeding. So I would like you to stop the omeprazole and the ibuprofen. For migraines you can use acetaminophen 500 mg as needed, and tell me if the heartburn comes back.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: For the iron, change the ferrous sulfate to 325 mg every other day, taken with water on an empty stomach at the start of your day, whatever your day is, even if that is after a night shift. Keep the sertraline 50 mg daily and the albuterol as needed.
Patient: Does it matter that I am asleep during the day?
Doctor: Take the iron when you wake up, away from coffee or tea. I am going to order an upper endoscopy with biopsies of the stomach and small bowel, and a stool test for H. pylori. We will schedule the endoscopy on a day off or right after a night shift, whichever you prefer, so you are not losing sleep. I will refer you to gynecology for the heavy periods, and we will repeat the blood count and ferritin in 8 weeks. If the hemoglobin does not improve, we will consider a colonoscopy and IV iron.
Patient: Okay, I will text the scheduler with my shifts.
"""

note:
Ambient scribe transcript. Gastroenterology outpatient clinic, evaluation of anemia in a 20-year-old female.

Doctor: Your primary care doctor sent you because your blood count showed low iron. What have you noticed?
Patient: I've been exhausted for months, and I get dizzy when I stand up fast. My friends say I look pale. I also keep craving ice, which sounds weird.
Doctor: How does your work schedule fit into this?
Patient: I work nights at a distribution center, three or four nights a week, but the schedule changes every week and sometimes they switch me to days. My sleep and my meals are all over the place.
Doctor: Any black or bloody stools?
Patient: No, never.
Doctor: Belly pain, diarrhea, or trouble swallowing?
Patient: No belly pain, no diarrhea, and swallowing is fine.
Doctor: Any weight loss?
Patient: No, my weight is the same.
Doctor: Tell me about your periods.
Patient: They are heavy. They last about seven days, and I soak a pad every two or three hours on the first two days, with some clots.
Doctor: What are you taking?
Patient: Ferrous sulfate 325 mg twice a day, omeprazole 20 mg every morning that I bought over the counter for heartburn, ibuprofen 400 mg when I get a migraine, sertraline 100 mg daily, and my albuterol inhaler for asthma.
Doctor: Let's go through the iron again. Twice a day?
Patient: Sorry, no. I only take the iron once a day, and I skip it on nights when I am rushing to work.
Doctor: And the sertraline? My list shows 50 mg.
Patient: Let me look at the bottle. You are right, it is 50 mg once a day.
Doctor: Thank you. Your vital signs today are blood pressure 104/62, heart rate 96, and oxygen saturation 99 percent. You look pale and your conjunctivae are pale. Your heart rhythm is regular with a soft flow murmur, your lungs are clear, and your abdomen is soft and not tender, with no liver or spleen enlargement. Your labs from last week show a hemoglobin of 9.1, an MCV of 74, and a ferritin of 6, which confirms iron deficiency. The celiac antibody, tissue transglutaminase IgA, was negative with a normal total IgA, and your pregnancy test was negative.
Patient: So what is causing it?
Doctor: My impression is iron-deficiency anemia, most likely from your heavy periods, but we also need to rule out a bleeding or absorption problem in the gut. The omeprazole and the ibuprofen can both make this worse, since the acid blocker reduces iron absorption and ibuprofen can irritate the stomach and cause bleeding. So I would like you to stop the omeprazole and the ibuprofen. For migraines you can use acetaminophen 500 mg as needed, and tell me if the heartburn comes back.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: For the iron, change the ferrous sulfate to 325 mg every other day, taken with water on an empty stomach at the start of your day, whatever your day is, even if that is after a night shift. Keep the sertraline 50 mg daily and the albuterol as needed.
Patient: Does it matter that I am asleep during the day?
Doctor: Take the iron when you wake up, away from coffee or tea. I am going to order an upper endoscopy with biopsies of the stomach and small bowel, and a stool test for H. pylori. We will schedule the endoscopy on a day off or right after a night shift, whichever you prefer, so you are not losing sleep. I will refer you to gynecology for the heavy periods, and we will repeat the blood count and ferritin in 8 weeks. If the hemoglobin does not improve, we will consider a colonoscopy and IV iron.
Patient: Okay, I will text the scheduler with my shifts.

Clinical note:
"""
Dermatology follow-up seen on the hospital ward for a 33-year-old male admitted three days ago with a left leg deep vein thrombosis, currently receiving apixaban 10 mg twice daily. The inpatient team asked for evaluation of facial redness and bumps that have been present for about two years and have worsened since admission. He describes flushing of the cheeks and nose with hot drinks and stress, along with intermittent stinging. He denies eye pain, denies blurred vision, and denies itching or fever.

On examination there is central facial erythema with scattered inflammatory papules and a few pustules over the cheeks, nose, and chin, and visible telangiectasias on both cheeks. No comedones are seen. There is no rhinophyma and the conjunctivae are clear. The patient is hemodynamically stable per the primary team.

The impression is papulopustular rosacea. Topical therapy is preferred while he is hospitalized and anticoagulated, so I started azelaic acid 15% gel twice daily to the affected areas of the face. I counseled him on gentle skin care, daily broad-spectrum sunscreen, and avoiding triggers such as hot drinks and alcohol. Laser treatment of the telangiectasias will be deferred until he is no longer on apixaban. Apixaban will continue at 10 mg twice daily per the primary team. He will follow up in the dermatology clinic in six weeks to assess his response.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Dermatology follow-up seen on the hospital ward for a 33-year-old male admitted three days ago with a left leg deep vein thrombosis, currently receiving apixaban 10 mg twice daily. The inpatient team asked for evaluation of facial redness and bumps that have been present for about two years and have worsened since admission. He describes flushing of the cheeks and nose with hot drinks and stress, along with intermittent stinging. He denies eye pain, denies blurred vision, and denies itching or fever.

On examination there is central facial erythema with scattered inflammatory papules and a few pustules over the cheeks, nose, and chin, and visible telangiectasias on both cheeks. No comedones are seen. There is no rhinophyma and the conjunctivae are clear. The patient is hemodynamically stable per the primary team.

The impression is papulopustular rosacea. Topical therapy is preferred while he is hospitalized and anticoagulated, so I started azelaic acid 15% gel twice daily to the affected areas of the face. I counseled him on gentle skin care, daily broad-spectrum sunscreen, and avoiding triggers such as hot drinks and alcohol. Laser treatment of the telangiectasias will be deferred until he is no longer on apixaban. Apixaban will continue at 10 mg twice daily per the primary team. He will follow up in the dermatology clinic in six weeks to assess his response.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 3 for this 72-year-old female with long-standing type 1 diabetes managed with an insulin pump, who was admitted after an episode of severe hypoglycemia at work. She works part-time as a hospital unit clerk on a rotating schedule of three night shifts and two day shifts per week with changing start times. Her coworker found her sweating and confused during a night shift, and EMS recorded a fingerstick glucose of 38 mg/dL. She received IV dextrose with prompt recovery and was admitted for evaluation and pump adjustment.

Overnight there was no further severe hypoglycemia. Her continuous glucose monitor showed a low of 68 mg/dL at about three in the morning, which she treated with 15 grams of juice, and the low alert sounded as programmed. She denies chest pain, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and alcohol use, and she reports no pump alarms or site problems.

She has had type 1 diabetes for over 40 years, with hypoglycemia unawareness, diabetic retinopathy, diabetic neuropathy, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, hypothyroidism, and hyperlipidemia. Home medications are insulin aspart by pump, metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. Her outside records listed the overnight basal rate as 0.9 units per hour, but the pump download shows it was 1.1 units per hour; the correct overnight basal rate is 1.1 units per hour, not 0.9. The download also shows an insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio of 1 to 8. On the day of the event she worked a day shift, slept only two hours, started a night shift, and took a meal bolus that she then did not finish while the overnight basal continued at full rate.

Vital signs today are temperature 98.2 F, heart rate 68, blood pressure 126/72, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She is alert and oriented with no focal deficits. The abdominal pump site is clean without erythema. Monofilament sensation is reduced in both feet. Laboratory data show A1c 6.4%, creatinine 1.2 with eGFR 47, potassium 4.4, sodium 139, TSH 2.8, and AM cortisol 15 mcg/dL. C-peptide is undetectable, consistent with her diagnosis. Continuous glucose monitor data over the past two weeks show time in range 61 percent, time below 70 mg/dL 14 percent, and time below 54 mg/dL 5 percent, with most lows between midnight and 5 in the morning on night-shift days.

Assessment is type 1 diabetes with frequent, severe hypoglycemia and hypoglycemia unawareness. Contributing factors are overly tight control for her age and comorbidities, a single pump profile that does not match her irregular work schedule, and metoprolol, which can mask the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia.

For management, I am reducing the overnight basal rate from 1.1 to 0.8 units per hour and changing the insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio from 1 to 8 to 1 to 10. We will build two pump profiles, one for day-shift days and one for night-shift days, that she can switch herself, with a higher glucose target on night shifts. The monitor low alert threshold will be raised to 80 mg/dL with the predictive low alert on and automatic suspend before low enabled. The new A1c goal is below 7.5 percent. I am discontinuing metoprolol tartrate and starting amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure. She will receive glucagon nasal 3 mg as needed for severe hypoglycemia, and her family and a coworker will be taught how to use it. Lisinopril 10 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly continue unchanged. The diabetes educator and dietitian will see her today for shift-work meal planning and hypoglycemia unawareness training, and she was advised not to drive if her glucose is below 90. Social work will help with a letter requesting a more regular schedule from her employer. She will follow up with endocrinology in one week, with a BMP recheck, and with ophthalmology as scheduled. Discharge is anticipated tomorrow if there are no further lows.
"""

She works rotating night and day shifts, and her A1c is 6.4% with 14 percent of CGM time below 70 mg/dL. The assessment was type 1 diabetes with frequent severe hypoglycemia and hypoglycemia unawareness from tight control, a single pump profile, and metoprolol masking symptoms. The overnight basal rate was reduced to 0.8 units per hour, separate day and night shift profiles were built, metoprolol was stopped, and amlodipine and glucagon were started.

Doctor: Good morning. I'm seeing you after your lab draw this morning. You're a 39-year-old female on chemotherapy for breast cancer, correct?
Patient: Yes, I had cycle three of doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide ten days ago.
Doctor: And I understand you just traveled. Tell me about that.
Patient: I flew home from an overseas trip five days ago. It was a long flight, about fourteen hours, and I stayed with relatives. I know I wasn't supposed to go, but it was a family emergency.
Doctor: How have you been feeling since you got back?
Patient: Tired, really tired, and I've had a mild sore throat for the last two days. My mouth feels sore too.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No fever. I checked this morning and it was 36.8. No chills either.
Doctor: Any cough, shortness of breath, diarrhea, or burning when you urinate?
Patient: No cough, no shortness of breath, and no burning. I had loose stools once while I was abroad, but it passed in a day.
Doctor: Any sick contacts on the flight or at your relatives' house?
Patient: My cousin had a cold, but nobody was seriously sick.
Doctor: Did you start any new medicines or supplements?
Patient: No, just my usual anti-nausea pills, ondansetron 8 mg. I take it as needed, maybe once a day since chemo.

There's no redness around your port site.
Patient: That's good.
Doctor: This is chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, and the travel adds some infection risk, so we need to be careful. I'm going to delay your next cycle by one week. I want to start filgrastim 480 mcg injected under the skin once a day until your neutrophil count recovers. My nurse will teach you to give the injection. We'll repeat your blood count in two days.

Patient: Okay. Should I keep taking the ondansetron?

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 3 progress note for a 48-year-old male admitted with severe retrosternal burning and regurgitation despite daily proton pump inhibitor therapy, now followed by gastroenterology for refractory gastroesophageal reflux disease. He works rotating night shifts at a distribution center, and his sleep and meal times shift from week to week. On working nights he typically eats a large meal around 3 am, and after his shift ends he goes to bed within an hour and sleeps flat during the day, which likely contributes to his symptoms.

Interval events: A cardiac cause was excluded on admission with two negative troponin measurements and a normal ECG. He underwent EGD yesterday, which showed LA grade B erosive esophagitis and a 3 cm hiatal hernia without Barrett's changes, and biopsies were taken from the distal esophagus and the stomach. He tolerated the procedure well. His burning chest pain is somewhat better today at 3 out of 10, compared with 8 out of 10 on admission. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, hematemesis, melena, fever, and unintentional weight loss. He has not had any exertional chest pain.

Medication reconciliation: On admission he told the team that he takes omeprazole 40 mg twice daily at home. His wife brought in his bottles today, and the label reads omeprazole 20 mg once daily, so correction, his home dose is omeprazole 20 mg once daily, not 40 mg twice daily. He takes it at irregular times, often with or after his first meal, and skips it on rushed nights. His reflux therefore persisted on low-dose once-daily therapy and not on maximal twice-daily therapy. Other home medications are lisinopril 20 mg daily for HTN, metformin 1000 mg twice daily for T2DM, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly for hyperlipidemia, and famotidine 20 mg at bedtime as needed. He also admits to taking ibuprofen 400 mg a few times a week for low back pain from lifting at work. He has no known drug allergies.

Current inpatient medications: pantoprazole 40 mg IV once daily since admission, along with his lisinopril, metformin, and atorvastatin.

Vital signs: Temp 36.9 C, HR 76, BP 138/84, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air. Weight 104 kg, BMI 34, consistent with obesity. He is comfortable on exam. The abdomen is obese and soft with mild epigastric tenderness and no guarding or rebound. Lungs are clear. There is no edema. Labs this morning: WBC 7.2, Hgb 14.2, Na 139, K 4.1, Cr 0.9, glucose 148. HbA1c from admission was 7.4%.

Impression: Refractory GERD with LA grade B erosive esophagitis and a 3 cm hiatal hernia. Contributors are his rotating night schedule with large late meals before lying flat, obesity, regular ibuprofen use, and suboptimal PPI use (low dose, once daily, and poorly timed). HTN, T2DM, and hyperlipidemia are stable.

Recommendations: Increase pantoprazole to 40 mg IV twice daily today, then transition to oral esomeprazole 40 mg twice daily at discharge, taken 30 minutes before his first meal after waking and again before his second main meal of the day, whatever clock time that falls at. Discontinue home omeprazole. Stop ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for back pain instead. Continue famotidine 20 mg at bedtime, taken before his daytime sleep period. Continue lisinopril, metformin, and atorvastatin without changes.

I counseled him to avoid eating within 3 hours of lying down, to eat smaller meals, to keep a consistent meal schedule anchored to his wake time, and to raise the head of the bed by 6 inches. A dietitian referral for meal planning around shift work and weight loss will be placed. We will follow up the esophageal and gastric biopsy pathology for Barrett's esophagus, eosinophilic esophagitis, and H. pylori. If symptoms persist after 8 weeks of twice-daily therapy, he will need 24-hour pH-impedance monitoring and referral for surgical evaluation of antireflux surgery. He is likely ready for discharge tomorrow if his pain remains controlled and he tolerates his diet. GI clinic follow-up in 6 to 8 weeks.
"""

History of present illness: This is an 80-year-old female who developed a proximal left leg deep vein thrombosis about 11 weeks ago, after a hospitalization for pneumonia with several days of bed rest. She was started on apixaban 5 mg twice daily and has not missed any doses. Her leg swelling has improved. She denies bleeding, black stools, new leg swelling, chest pain, and shortness of breath. She has no history of previous clots or cancer.

Examination: Blood pressure 128/76, HR 70, SpO2 97% on room air. There is mild residual swelling of the left calf, about 1 cm larger than the right, without tenderness, warmth, or redness.

Data reviewed: Hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelets 238, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. The duplex ultrasound at diagnosis showed thrombus in the left femoral vein.

Impression: Provoked left leg deep vein thrombosis that is improving on apixaban, with a major transient risk factor (hospitalization with immobility) and no bleeding on therapy.

Recommendations: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily to complete a total of 3 months, then stop. Repeat a duplex ultrasound of the left leg before stopping to document the residual clot. No thrombophilia testing is needed. Counsel on bleeding precautions and return precautions for new swelling, chest pain, or shortness of breath. Hematology follow-up only if symptoms recur.

Clinical note:
"""
Telehealth visit via secure video. Patient is at home with her daughter in the room. Verbal consent for the video visit obtained. 57-year-old female with hidradenitis suppurativa, here for follow-up of a flare.

History: Patient reports painful, draining nodules in the left axilla and both groin folds for about 3 weeks, worse than her usual baseline. Her daughter, who helps with dressing changes every day, adds that the bandages are soaked twice a day now and that her mother has been waking at night because of the pain, although her mother tends to downplay it. Patient rates the pain 7 out of 10. She denies fever, denies chills, denies spreading redness beyond the lesions, and denies new lesions on the buttocks. She smokes about half a pack of cigarettes a day. She has type 2 diabetes. Current medications are metformin 1000 mg BID and clindamycin 1% lotion applied BID to the affected areas, used for 8 weeks with little benefit. She takes ibuprofen 400 mg as needed for pain. No known drug allergies.

Home measurements: temperature 98.4 F, BP 132/80, pulse 82 on her home cuff. A1c from her primary care doctor last month was 7.8%. Wound culture from the left axilla at the previous visit grew methicillin-sensitive Staph aureus.

Exam by video, limited, with the daughter holding the tablet: left axilla has 3 tender inflamed nodules and one draining sinus tract with surrounding scarring, no streaking or spreading erythema. Right axilla has old scarring without active lesions. Groin folds seen briefly, with two inflamed nodules on the right and one on the left. Patient is comfortable and speaking in full sentences.

Impression: Hurley stage II hidradenitis suppurativa with an active flare of the left axilla and both groin folds. Type 2 diabetes with suboptimal control. Tobacco use, which worsens the disease.

Plan:
Stop clindamycin lotion since it has not helped.
Start doxycycline 100 mg BID for 12 weeks, taken with food and a full glass of water, with counseling on sun sensitivity.
Continue metformin and ibuprofen as needed.
Daughter instructed on non-adherent absorbent dressings and warm compresses.
Smoking cessation counseling provided and patient will think about nicotine replacement.
Repeat A1c with her primary care doctor in 2 months.
In-person visit in 4 weeks to consider intralesional triamcinolone injection and discuss adalimumab if no improvement.
Return sooner for fever or spreading redness.
"""

Blood pressure today is 138 over 84, heart rate 74, and weight is stable. On exam there is no peripheral edema, the lungs are clear, and the heart sounds are regular. Labs drawn today show creatinine 2.2 mg/dL with an eGFR of 38, potassium 4.7, bicarbonate 22, and a urine albumin to creatinine ratio of 210 mg/g. Compared with six months ago his kidney function is unchanged. Impression is chronic kidney disease stage 3b, stable, with moderately increased albuminuria and blood pressure slightly above goal. Plan is to increase lisinopril to 40 mg once daily. Because travel is difficult, he will have a basic metabolic panel drawn at a laboratory near his home two weeks after the dose change, and I will review the result by phone. """
Dictation for outpatient neurology follow-up. The patient is a 41-year-old female with young onset Parkinson's disease, diagnosed three years ago, correction, four years ago, who comes in for routine follow-up. Over the past two months she reports that each dose of her levodopa seems to wear off about an hour before the next one is due, and during that time she gets stiffness and slowness in the right arm and leg and a return of the tremor in her right hand. She also reports lightheadedness when she stands up quickly and ongoing constipation. She denies falls, hallucinations, compulsive gambling, trouble swallowing, and daytime sleepiness. Her mood has been stable and she is still working full time.

Current medications are carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg, one tablet three times daily, pramipexole 0.5 mg three times daily, rasagiline 1 mg once daily, and polyethylene glycol 17 grams daily as needed for constipation.

Orthostatic vital signs: seated blood pressure 118/72 with heart rate 78, and after three minutes standing blood pressure 104/66 with heart rate 88. On exam she has mild hypomimia, a resting tremor in the right hand, mild rigidity of the right arm with cogwheeling, and bradykinesia with right finger tapping. Her gait is steady with decreased arm swing on the right, turns are smooth, and the pull test is normal. Strength and sensation are normal. Labs from last month showed hemoglobin 13.4, creatinine 0.8, and TSH 1.8.

My impression is Parkinson's disease with early wearing off motor fluctuations, and mild orthostatic hypotension, most likely related to her dopaminergic medications. For the plan, I will change carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg from three times daily to four times daily, spaced about four hours apart and taken thirty minutes before meals. Continue pramipexole and rasagiline at the current doses. Increase fluids and dietary salt, rise slowly from sitting, and consider compression stockings. Continue polyethylene glycol and add more fiber. Check a vitamin B12 level. Refer to physical therapy and occupational therapy for gait and hand function training. Return to clinic in three months, sooner if falls or hallucinations.
"""

Patient: Yes. It started this morning in my back on the right side and it comes in waves. It goes down toward my groin, and I threw up twice.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No fever and no chills.
Doctor: Any burning when you pee, or blood in the urine?
Patient: No burning, but my urine looked pink this morning.
Doctor: Have you ever had a kidney stone before?
Patient: No, never.
Doctor: Any medical problems, and what medicines do you take?
Patient: I have high blood pressure and I take lisinopril 10 mg every day.
Doctor: Any allergies to medications?
Patient: Yes, I'm allergic to ibuprofen. I get hives and my lips swell up.
Doctor: Thank you, that's important. I will not give you ibuprofen, ketorolac, or any other anti-inflammatory pain medicine. Is there any chance you could be pregnant?

Patient: It hurts when you press on my back there.
Doctor: Your urinalysis shows blood but no signs of infection, and your pregnancy test is negative. The CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis shows a 5 mm stone in the right ureter with mild swelling of the kidney, which is called hydronephrosis. Your creatinine is 0.9, so your kidney function is normal.
Patient: Okay. Can I get something for the pain? I feel sick to my stomach too.
Doctor: Yes. I am going to give you acetaminophen 1000 mg by IV, ondansetron 4 mg IV for the nausea, and morphine 4 mg IV for the severe pain.
Patient: Thank you.
Doctor: My impression is a kidney stone causing renal colic. A 5 mm stone has a good chance of passing on its own. You will go home with tamsulosin 0.4 mg once a day to help the stone pass and acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed for pain. Drink plenty of fluids and strain your urine. Please follow up with urology in one week. Come back right away for fever, pain you cannot control, or if you cannot keep fluids down.
Patient: Okay, I understand.
"""

"""
The patient is a 34-year-old male seen in orthopedic clinic for follow-up of a right rotator cuff tear. He works as a warehouse loader and first noticed right shoulder pain about eight weeks ago after lifting a heavy pallet overhead. He describes a deep ache in the lateral shoulder that wakes him at night when he rolls onto the right side, along with weakness when reaching overhead. He denies numbness, tingling, neck pain, or shoulder instability. He has not had fever or any prior shoulder surgery.

Since his last visit he has attended only one of four scheduled physical therapy sessions. He depends on the bus, the trip takes about ninety minutes each way, and he has lost work shifts to attend visits. We discussed that transportation is the main barrier to his follow-up and rehabilitation.

Medical history is notable for hypertension, for which he takes lisinopril 10 mg daily. For the shoulder pain he has been taking naproxen 500 mg twice daily, which he received from urgent care.

On examination today his blood pressure is 148/92, heart rate 76, and he is afebrile. There is mild supraspinatus atrophy on the right. Passive range of motion is full, but active elevation is limited to about 120 degrees by pain, with a painful arc between 90 and 120 degrees. Hawkins and empty can tests are positive, and supraspinatus strength is 4/5. The Spurling test is negative, and sensation and distal pulses are intact.

An MRI of the right shoulder obtained last month shows a partial-thickness articular-sided supraspinatus tear involving roughly 40 percent of the tendon thickness, mild infraspinatus tendinosis, no retraction, and no labral tear. Radiographs today show a type II acromion with no fracture or arthritis.

Impression is a right rotator cuff tear, partial thickness, with ongoing pain and weakness, and elevated blood pressure that is likely aggravated by naproxen in the setting of hypertension. After verbal consent, a subacromial corticosteroid injection with triamcinolone 40 mg and lidocaine 1 percent was performed today and he tolerated it well. I am stopping naproxen and starting acetaminophen 1,000 mg every 8 hours as needed. He will continue lisinopril 10 mg daily and have his blood pressure rechecked by his primary care clinic within two weeks. He was given a home exercise program with a resistance band, and we will arrange telehealth physical therapy visits so that he does not need to travel. Social work will help him apply for the non-emergency medical transportation benefit through his insurance. A video check-in will occur in two weeks and an in-person visit in six weeks, scheduled on a day when he already has transportation. If he is not improving by three months we will discuss surgical repair. He should call sooner for worsening weakness or numbness.
"""

He was counseled to keep the lesions covered, avoid contact with infants, immunocompromised people, and anyone who has not had chickenpox until the lesions crust, and wash his hands often. Hospitalist progress note, dictated on hospital day 3 for a 44-year-old male admitted with an upper gastrointestinal bleed. Overnight events, none. He had been taking ibuprofen 600 mg three times a day for low back pain. He works night shifts at a warehouse with a rotating schedule, which is why he went so long without seeing anyone and why his meals and sleep are irregular. He has no known drug allergies.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy on hospital day 1 showed a duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel, treated with epinephrine injection and hemoclip placement. A rapid urease test was positive for Helicobacter pylori. He received one unit of packed red blood cells for a hemoglobin of 7.6, and the most recent hemoglobin this morning is 8.2, correction, 8.4. BUN has improved to 18, creatinine 0.9, INR 1.0, and platelets 245.

The intravenous pantoprazole course is complete, so I am changing him to oral pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily. Diet advanced to regular. Repeat hemoglobin in the morning, and if stable he can be discharged tomorrow with a work excuse letter. He will follow up with gastroenterology in four weeks, and a test to confirm Helicobacter pylori eradication should be done at least four weeks after the antibiotics.
"""
